*Lecture 20 · [[7-transformers/index|Transformers]] · builds on [[7-transformers/attention|attention]] and [[7-transformers/text-encodings-and-embeddings|embeddings]] · part of the [[7-transformers/transformer-architecture|Full Transformer]]*

> [!abstract] In one breath
> Attention compares every token with every other token but never asks **where** they are: shuffle the input words and self-attention returns the same vectors, shuffled. To give the model word order, the Transformer **adds** a position-dependent vector $p_{pos}\in\mathbb R^{d}$ to each token's embedding before the first layer. The paper's choice is a set of sines and cosines whose wavelengths grow geometrically from $2\pi$ to $10000\cdot2\pi$ across the dimensions, so every position gets a distinct, bounded vector and shifting by $k$ positions is a fixed rotation. Learned position embeddings work about as well. In Lecture 20's ablation, removing positional encoding costs about 0.05 validation BLEU; sinusoidal and learned are indistinguishable.

## What it is

### Attention does not see order

Let $P$ be a permutation matrix that reorders the $N$ tokens of $Z\in\mathbb R^{N\times d}$. Self-attention on the reordered input has $Q' = PQ$, $K' = PK$, $V' = PV$, so the score matrix becomes $PQK^\top P^\top$: the same scores with rows and columns permuted alike. A row-wise softmax commutes with that, giving $A' = PAP^\top$, and

$$
\mathrm{Attention}(PZ) = PAP^\top\,PV = P\,AV = P\,\mathrm{Attention}(Z)\qquad(P^\top P = I).
$$

Self-attention is **permutation-equivariant**: permuting the input permutes the output the same way and changes nothing else. The feed-forward network and layer norm act on each token separately, so they are equivariant too. Cross-attention is even **invariant** to the order of the source tokens: permuting keys and values together gives $AP^\top\,PV = AV$. Without positions, the encoder sees "the dog bites the man" and "the man bites the dog" as the same bag of words.

(The decoder's [[7-transformers/attention#masked-self-attention|causal mask]] breaks the symmetry a little: position 0 can only attend to itself, position 1 to two tokens, and so on, which leaks some order information. That is one reason the "no positional encoding" model below still learns something.)

### Adding a position vector

> [!definition] Definition — positional encoding
> A function $pos\mapsto p_{pos}\in\mathbb R^{d_{emb}}$ for $pos = 0, 1, 2, \dots$, added to the token embeddings at the bottom of the encoder and of the decoder: $z_{pos} \leftarrow z_{pos} + p_{pos}$. It should give every position a **distinct** vector, stay bounded, and make nearby positions look alike.

The vectors are **added**, not concatenated, so the model width stays $d_{emb}$. The course's encoder does it in one line:

```python
z = self.embedding(x).squeeze(1)
z = z + self.position_encoding(z)    # add p_pos to row pos
```

## What you should know

- Why attention needs positional information (equivariance/invariance argument above) while RNNs and CNNs get order for free.
- The paper's formula, and that each sine/cosine **pair** shares one frequency $\omega_j = 10000^{-2j/d}$; wavelengths form a geometric progression from $2\pi$ to $10000\cdot2\pi$.
- What the heatmap shows: fast oscillation in low dimensions, almost constant high dimensions, a distinct row per position.
- Relative positions: $p_{pos+k}$ is a fixed linear function (a rotation per frequency pair) of $p_{pos}$, and $p_{pos}\cdot p_{pos+k}$ depends only on $k$.
- Learned positional embeddings: an `nn.Embedding(max_len, d)` indexed by position; similar results, but no positions beyond `max_len`.
- The Lecture 20 ablation numbers and what they show.

## The sinusoidal encoding

> [!key] Paper (Vaswani et al., 2017, §3.5)
> $$
> PE_{(pos,\,2j)} = \sin\!\Bigl(\frac{pos}{10000^{2j/d}}\Bigr),\qquad PE_{(pos,\,2j+1)} = \cos\!\Bigl(\frac{pos}{10000^{2j/d}}\Bigr),\qquad j = 0,1,\dots,\tfrac d2-1.
> $$
> Dimensions $2j$ and $2j+1$ are a sine and a cosine of the **same** angle $\omega_j\,pos$, with $\omega_j = 10000^{-2j/d}$.

The lecture writes it per dimension index $i$, with the exponent $i/d$ for **both** parities:

$$
p[i] = \begin{cases}\sin\bigl(pos/10000^{i/d}\bigr) & i \text{ even}\\ \cos\bigl(pos/10000^{i/d}\bigr) & i \text{ odd.}\end{cases}
$$

Even dimensions agree with the paper ($i = 2j$). An odd dimension $i = 2j+1$ uses exponent $(2j+1)/d$ instead of $2j/d$: its frequency is $10000^{-1/d}$ times its partner's (0.93 for $d = 128$). Both versions give distinct positions and train equally well in practice; only the exact pairing (and the rotation property below) belongs to the paper's version. The course's code follows the lecture formula:

```python
d = self.embedding_dim
L = len(x)
p = torch.tensor([[np.sin(pos/(10000**(i/d))) if (i%2==0) else np.cos(pos/(10000**(i/d))) \
                   for i in range(d)] for pos in range(L)]).to(DEVICE)
```

### Worked example, $d = 4$

| $pos$ | paper $(\sin, \cos, \sin, \cos)$ | lecture |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | $(0, 1, 0, 1)$ | $(0, 1, 0, 1)$ |
| 1 | $(\sin 1, \cos 1, \sin 0.01, \cos 0.01) = (0.841, 0.540, 0.010, 1.000)$ | $(0.841, \cos 0.1, 0.010, \cos 0.001) = (0.841, 0.995, 0.010, 1.000)$ |
| 2 | $(0.909, -0.416, 0.020, 1.000)$ | $(0.909, 0.980, 0.020, 1.000)$ |

The first pair turns through one radian per position; the second pair through 0.01 radian ($10000^{2/4} = 100$).

Dimension <i>i</i> oscillates with wavelength 2π·10000<sup><i>i</i>/<i>d</i></sup> (lecture formula, <i>d</i> = 128): about 6 positions for <i>i</i> = 0 and 7 for <i>i</i> = 1 (a sine and a cosine of almost the same frequency), 26 for <i>i</i> = 20, 471 for <i>i</i> = 60. Over a 25-token sentence the high dimensions are nearly constant.</figcaption></figure>

> [!intuition] A clock with many hands
> Think of each frequency pair as a clock hand that turns by $\omega_j$ radians per position: the first hand spins fast (a full turn every $2\pi\approx6.3$ positions), the last one barely moves (one turn in about 54,000 positions for $d = 128$). The positions of all the hands together identify the position uniquely, much like the digits of a binary counter, but smoothly. The lecture describes the frequencies as increasing "linearly along the position dimension"; more precisely, each dimension's **angle** grows linearly with position, while the **frequency** shrinks geometrically from one dimension pair to the next.

### Why sinusoids: relative positions are linear

For one frequency pair, with $a = \omega_j\,pos$ and $b = \omega_j k$,

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\sin(a+b)\\ \cos(a+b)\end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix}\cos b & \sin b\\ -\sin b & \cos b\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}\sin a\\ \cos a\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The matrix depends on the offset $k$ but **not** on $pos$, so $PE_{pos+k} = R_k\,PE_{pos}$ with $R_k$ block-diagonal (one $2\times2$ rotation per pair). This is the paper's stated motivation: "for any fixed offset $k$, $PE_{pos+k}$ can be represented as a linear function of $PE_{pos}$", which should make it easy for attention's linear projections to attend by relative position. Two consequences, checked numerically for $d = 128$:

- $\lVert PE_{pos}\rVert = \sqrt{d/2} = 8$ for every position (each pair has $\sin^2+\cos^2 = 1$).
- $PE_{pos}\cdot PE_{pos+k} = \sum_j \cos(\omega_j k)$ depends only on $k$: 64.0, 62.1, 57.4, 52.2, 48.6 for $k = 0,\dots,4$, from any starting position. Nearby positions have similar vectors.

With the lecture's odd-dimension frequencies the two members of a pair turn at different rates, so the exact rotation identity no longer holds.

The paper adds a second reason to prefer sinusoids: they are defined for any position, so they "may allow the model to extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than the ones encountered during training".

## Learned positional embeddings

The alternative is to learn $p_{pos}$ like a word embedding: a table with one row per position.

```python
if mode == 'learned':
    self.embedding = nn.Embedding(MAX_LENGTH, embedding_dim)    # 25 x 128
...
p = torch.arange(len(x)).unsqueeze(1)
p = self.embedding(p).squeeze(1)
```

It adds $25\cdot128 = 3{,}200$ parameters per side, and it cannot represent a position $\ge 25$ (an index error for longer inputs). The paper tried learned embeddings and "found that the two versions produced nearly identical results" (Table 3, row E: 25.7 vs 25.8 BLEU on the development set).

Sinusoidal and learned encodings track each other; with no positional information validation BLEU levels off about 0.05 lower.</figcaption></figure>

| Positional encoding | Train BLEU | **Val BLEU** (max) | Final loss |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| sinusoidal | 0.75 | **0.45** (0.47) | 0.26 |
| learned | 0.75 | 0.44 (0.47) | 0.26 |
| none | 0.68 | 0.40 (0.41) | 0.33 |

(BLEU: mean of the last five evaluations; loss: mean of the last ten logged values.) Sinusoidal and learned are within run-to-run noise of each other; without positions the model both fits worse (higher loss, lower training BLEU) and generalizes worse. The lecture's conclusion: "any reasonable positional encoding performs similarly, but the inclusion of positional encoding is nonetheless important." Positional encoding is also most of the gain from [[7-transformers/transformer-architecture#results|Medium to Full]]: the no-encoding Full model (0.40) is close to the Medium model (0.38).

> [!trap] Common mistakes
> - **Concatenating instead of adding.** The encoding is added, so it must have the embedding's size $d_{emb}$.
> - **Adding it once, in the middle.** It goes in at the bottom of both the encoder and the decoder, before the first attention layer.
> - **Mixing up the axes.** Along the position axis each dimension is a sinusoid with a fixed frequency; across dimensions the frequency drops geometrically.
> - **Learned table too short.** A learned encoding sized `MAX_LENGTH` fails on longer inputs; sinusoids do not.
> - **Course code quirks.** With `mode=None` the class returns `p = x`, so `z + p` doubles the embedding instead of adding nothing: no position information, as intended, just a scaled embedding. In `'learned'` mode `torch.arange(len(x))` is created on the CPU, which breaks on a GPU unless moved to `DEVICE`. The sinusoidal table is rebuilt in Python on every forward call; implementations usually compute it once and store it with [`register_buffer`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.Module.html#torch.nn.Module.register_buffer).

> [!question]- Check yourself
> 1. Swap the first two words of an encoder input with no positional encoding. What happens to the encoder output? To the decoder's prediction?
> 2. With the paper's formula and $d = 512$, what are the wavelengths of dimensions 0–1 and 510–511?
> 3. Show that $PE_{pos}\cdot PE_{pos+k}$ does not depend on $pos$ (paper version).
>
> > [!solution]- Answers
> > 1. The encoder's output rows 0 and 1 swap and nothing else changes (equivariance). Cross-attention is invariant to the order of keys/values, so the decoder's prediction is exactly the same.
> > 2. Pair $j = 0$: $\omega_0 = 1$, wavelength $2\pi\approx6.3$. Pair $j = 255$: $\omega = 10000^{-510/512}$, wavelength $2\pi\cdot10000^{510/512}\approx 6.1\times10^4$ (just under $10000\cdot2\pi\approx6.3\times10^4$).
> > 3. Each pair contributes $\sin(\omega a)\sin(\omega(a+k)) + \cos(\omega a)\cos(\omega(a+k)) = \cos(\omega k)$, so the dot product is $\sum_j\cos(\omega_j k)$.

## PyTorch docs

- PyTorch has no built-in positional-encoding module; build it from [`torch.arange`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.arange.html), [`torch.sin`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.sin.html), [`torch.cos`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.cos.html) and [`torch.pow`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.pow.html).
- [`torch.nn.Embedding`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.Embedding.html) — learned positional embeddings (index by position, not by token).
- [`torch.nn.Module.register_buffer`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.Module.html#torch.nn.Module.register_buffer) — store a fixed table so it moves with `.to(device)` but is not trained.
- [The Annotated Transformer](https://nlp.seas.harvard.edu/annotated-transformer/) has a vectorized `PositionalEncoding` module in the paper's form.
